t.1.36.2: What is the reason that this name of Jaratkāru is renowned on earth? You should properly tell the etymology of Jaratkāru.
t.1.36.1: Śaunaka said: O son of the Sūta, you spoke the name Jaratkāru; I wish to hear about that great-souled seer.
t.1.36.3: Jarā, they say, means wasting away, and what is dreadful is called kāru. His body was kāru, dreadful, and that body the wise one slowly, little by little,
t.1.36.5: Thus addressed, the righteous-souled Śaunaka then laughed, and, addressing Ugraśravas, he said, "It is fitting."
t.1.36.4: He wasted his body away through fierce austerity, and that is why, O brahmin, he is called Jaratkāru; the sister of Vāsuki was named so in the same way.
t.1.36.6: Then, for a long time, that sage of rigorous vows, wise and devoted to austerity, did not desire a wife.
t.1.36.7: Chaste, devoted to austerity, given to the study of the Veda, and free from fear and weariness, that great-souled one roamed the whole earth, and he did not desire a wife even in his mind.
t.1.36.8: Then, when some later time had arrived, there was a king renowned as Parikṣit, upholder of the Kaurava lineage.
t.1.36.9: Just as Pāṇḍu, his great-grandfather of old, the mighty-armed one, the best of bowmen on earth, was devoted to hunting.
t.1.36.10: The lord of the earth roamed about, piercing deer and boars, hyenas and buffaloes, and various other wild beasts.
t.1.36.12: Just as the blessed Rudra, having pierced the sacrifice-deer in the sky, followed after it, bow in hand, searching for it here and there.
t.1.36.11: Once, having pierced a deer with a smooth-jointed arrow, he took up his bow and pursued it from behind through the dense forest.
t.1.36.13: For no deer pierced by him ever goes on living into the forest; surely it was a portent of his going to heaven, that the deer pierced by that king Parikṣit vanished.
t.1.36.14: Drawn far away by that deer, the lord of the earth, exhausted and tormented by thirst, came upon a sage in the forest.
t.1.36.16: Overcome by hunger and fatigue, the king rushed swiftly up to that sage of rigorous vows and, raising his bow, questioned the muni.
t.1.36.15: He was seated in the grazing grounds of the cows, living chiefly on the foam that flowed from the mouths of the calves as they drank their milk.
t.1.36.17: Ho there, O Brahmin! I am King Parikṣit, the son of Abhimanyu. A deer pierced by me has vanished; have you perhaps seen it?
t.1.36.18: That sage, abiding in his vow of silence, said nothing at all to him; the king, enraged, hung a dead snake upon his shoulder.
t.1.36.20: The king, casting off his anger and distressed at seeing him in that state, went back to the city, but the ṛṣi remained sitting just as he was.
t.1.36.19: Lifting it up with the tip of his bow, he gazed at him; but he said nothing at all to him, whether good or bad.
t.1.36.21: He had a young son, Śṛṅgī by name, of fierce energy and great austerity, very wrathful, hard to appease, and strict in his vows.
t.1.36.22: He, well restrained, waited upon Brahmā, the supreme god and lord, who delights in the welfare of all beings, at each appointed time. Then, permitted by Brahmā, he went home.
t.1.36.23: There, it is said, that son of the seer, hot-tempered, exceedingly wrathful and like poison, was spoken to in jest by his friend Kṛśa, a seer's son, who was playing and laughing, O best of the twice-born.
t.1.36.24: The father of you, who are so full of fiery energy and likewise so rich in austerities, carries a corpse upon his shoulder. Do not be proud, Śṛṅgin!
t.1.36.25: When the sons of seers, men like us, perfected, knowers of brahman and ascetics, are speaking, you must not utter a single word.
t.1.36.26: Where now is your pride in your manhood, where are those arrogant words of yours, you who will see your father bearing a corpse like this?
